The '''1744 [[FLLA]] World Cup''' was the 19th edition of the [[FLLA World Cup]], the quadrennial international [[Arraby]] tournament contested by the senior men's national teams of the member associations of the [[FLLA]]. It was held in [[Lycroa]] across [[Ayuma]] from 6 June to 4 July 1744, and was won by the hosts [[Lycroa]], who defeated [[Easuhura]] 0–0 ''(3–0 pens)'' in the final at the Estadio Huifarn in [[Huifarn]] to claim their fifth FLLA World Cup title and extend their record as the most successful nation in the competition's history. Thirty-two nations qualified for the final tournament, drawn from the seven continental confederations of the [[FLLA]], and contested 64 matches across seven host venues.

The 1744 edition was the first FLLA World Cup held under the FLLA's '''confederation rotation policy''', adopted by the FLLA Council in 1740, which reserved the hosting rights for each cycle to a single nominated confederation in turn. Under the policy the 1744 tournament fell to the [[AYFVL]], returning the World Cup to [[Ayuma]] for the first time since the [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 edition]]. The selection of [[Lycroa]] as host carried a significance well beyond the sporting calendar: the Federal Republic of Lycroa had completed the integration of the former [[State of Lycroa]] only in September 1738 under the [[Lycroan reunification]], six years before the opening match, and the bid programme presented to the [[AYFVL]] and the [[FLLA]] Council was framed throughout as a showcase of the reunified Lycroan state. [[Lycroa]] entered the competition itself as runners-up at the [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 edition]], having lost the final 2–1 to [[New Misos]] at the Vulna Olympic Stadium four years earlier; the 1744 final between the hosts [[Lycroa]] and [[Easuhura]] was widely framed in advance as both a redemption fixture for the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] generation defeated at Vulna and as the closing showpiece of [[Lycroa|Lycroa's]] first quadrennial cycle as a fully reunified state.

The competition is remembered as one of the most defensively played in FLLA World Cup history. A total of 169 goals were scored in 64 matches at an average of 2.64 per match, the second-lowest goal-per-match average then recorded at any FLLA World Cup, lower only than the 2.30 per match average of the [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 edition]], and the final between [[Lycroa]] and [[Easuhura]] produced no goal across 120 minutes of normal time and extra time before [[Lycroa]] converted each of the three penalties taken in the resulting shoot-out to lift the trophy 3–0. The leading individual goalscorer was [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] forward Galari Mestrei with six personal strikes; the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] captain and central midfielder Cario Velarzo, appearing at his fourth FLLA World Cup and setting the all-tournament record for repeat appearances at the time, received the FLLA Vairan Ball as the tournament's best player.

The 1744 tournament was also notable for the introduction of the standardised four-pot seeded draw under FLLA Council resolution 1743/4, the formalisation of the host-association exemption from binding qualifying fixtures, and the largest live-radio broadcasting coverage of any FLLA World Cup to that date. It produced one widely cited shock result in the group stage, the 4–1 defeat of the [[NAFVL]] qualifying winners [[United Delet]] by the [[ACFVL]] qualifier [[Areoix Lie]] at the Estadio Huifarn on 14 June, recorded across a pre-tournament FLLA-ranking gap of 215 points and described in the FLLA Tactical Review Committee's 1744 report as the most significant upset by ranking margin in the modern history of the competition.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/tactical-review/1744-report|title=Report of the FLLA Tactical Review Committee on the 1744 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=22 November 1744}}</ref>

==Host selection==
{{Main|1744 FLLA World Cup bids}}

The [[AYFVL]]-backed bid from [[Lycroa]] was confirmed as host of the 1744 FLLA World Cup by the [[FLLA]] Council on 18 March 1741, ending a bidding process that had been conducted entirely within the AYFVL secretariat under the confederation-rotation policy adopted by the FLLA Council on 4 February 1740. Under the rotation policy, hosting rights for the 1744 cycle were reserved to the [[AYFVL]] in its capacity as the continental association of the previous Ayuma-hosted edition's organising body; the FLLA Council retained the right of final approval over the candidate proposed by the rotating confederation, but no rival bid could be entertained from a confederation outside the rotation in any given cycle.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/news/1741/host-selection-lycroa|title=Lycroa confirmed as 1744 FLLA World Cup hosts|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 March 1741}}</ref>

The AYFVL secretariat received formal expressions of interest from three member associations during the bidding window opened in May 1740: [[Lycroa]], [[Praesyu]] and [[Easuhura]]. The [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] bid, formally submitted in September 1740 under the umbrella of the Lycroan Arraby Federation, prevailed over the rival proposals at the AYFVL Council meeting of 7 January 1741 by a vote of nine member associations to four, with two abstentions; the [[Praesyu|Praesyuan]] bid was withdrawn on the morning of the vote after a procedural complaint by the [[Easuhura|Easuhuran]] delegation was sustained by the AYFVL secretary. The FLLA Council ratified the AYFVL recommendation at its meeting of 18 March 1741, with [[Lycroa]] selected partly on the strength of its proposed seven-venue stadium programme and partly on the basis of its proximity to the centres of established [[AYFVL]] support across the eastern half of [[Ayuma]].

The Lycroan bid documentation presented to the [[AYFVL]] in September 1740 framed the proposed 1744 tournament expressly as a national showcase of the reunified Federal Republic. The bid declared the tournament an "instrument of the new federal settlement", referenced the [[Lycroan reunification]] of September 1738 by name in its opening pages, and committed the host federation to a seven-city venue programme deliberately spread across both the historic southern federal heartland (Huifarn, Dacorca, Sorvaya, Tianco) and the territories of the former [[State of Lycroa]] in the north (Tatuiro, Fujanza, Liambra). The AYFVL secretariat's technical assessment endorsed this territorial framing as a "fully federal" venue plan, distinguishing it from the more geographically concentrated [[Praesyu|Praesyuan]] and [[Easuhura|Easuhuran]] proposals. Within the [[FLLA]] Council, the [[Raledria|Raledrian]] and [[Dahe|Dahen]] delegations cited the [[Trundenn Statement]] and their support for reunification in 1737 as part of their open argument in favour of confirming the Lycroan candidacy.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.larf.ly/1740/bid-foreword|title=Foreword to the Lycroan bid for the 1744 FLLA World Cup|publisher=Lycroan Arraby Federation|date=12 September 1740}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/news/1741/raledria-dahe-support|title=Raledrian and Dahen statements on the Lycroan candidacy|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=20 March 1741}}</ref>

The total infrastructure budget pledged by the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] federal government and the participating municipalities was {{lahn}}640&nbsp;million, of which {{lahn}}180&nbsp;million was directed towards transport upgrades, principally the [[Huifarn]]–[[Dacorca]] coastal rail corridor and arterial road improvements connecting the seven host cities, and a further {{lahn}}95&nbsp;million was directed towards the reconstruction and upgrade of stadium and transport infrastructure in the constituent states of the former [[State of Lycroa]] under the post-reunification federal investment programme. A separate operational budget of {{lahn}}120&nbsp;million was allocated to security, broadcasting infrastructure and the volunteer programme. The total budget of {{lahn}}760&nbsp;million was the largest single-host budget recorded at an FLLA World Cup to that date and was approved by the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] federal parliament under the same vote that confirmed the federal capital expenditure programme for the post-reunification financial year 1741.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ayfvl.org/1741/lycroa-bid-summary|title=Summary of the successful Lycroan bid for the 1744 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[AYFVL]]|date=20 March 1741}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.larf.ly/1741/budget-statement|title=Federal budget statement of the Lycroan Arraby Federation for the 1744 FLLA World Cup|publisher=Lycroan Arraby Federation|date=4 April 1741}}</ref>

==Participating teams and officials==

===Qualification===
{{Main|1744 FLLA World Cup qualification}}

A total of 32 places at the tournament were allocated across the seven continental confederations of the [[FLLA]]. Each confederation administered its own qualifying competition, with the format reflecting the size of its membership and its allocation of finals berths. The host association [[Lycroa]] qualified as of right under FLLA hosting regulations and additionally took part in the [[AYFVL]] qualifying tournament in a non-binding capacity; [[Lycroa]] were placed in AYFVL qualifying Group A but their results were treated as friendlies for the purpose of advancement, and the seven binding qualification places allocated to the [[AYFVL]] were therefore divided between the seven non-host group winners. The defending champions [[New Misos]], winners of the [[1740 FLLA World Cup]], qualified through the [[ATFVL]] qualifiers on merit.

The 1744 qualification programme was the first under FLLA's standardised confederation-rotation framework. The reorganisation increased the [[AYFVL]] allocation from six binding places to seven (including the host), the [[MSFVL]] allocation from three to five, and reduced the [[ATFVL]] allocation from five places to four; the four other confederations each received an unchanged allocation of four places.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1742/berth-allocation-1744|title=Continental berth allocation for the 1744 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=15 September 1742}}</ref> The qualifying tournaments are summarised below; full results are recorded on the individual confederation pages.

===Final draw===
{{Main|1744 FLLA World Cup seeding}}

The final draw for the group stage was held at the Lycroan National Theatre in [[Huifarn]] on 4 December 1743, six months before the opening match. The 32 qualified teams were divided into four pots of eight on the basis of their pre-tournament [[FLLA]] rankings, with the host [[Lycroa]] and the seven highest-ranked sides ([[New Misos]], [[Easuhura]], [[Verusa]], [[Etirha]], [[Finae]], [[Quidic]] and [[Sanagara]]) placed in the seeded pot. The three remaining pots were arranged on geographical lines so as to maximise the continental diversity of each group; under the procedure approved by the FLLA Council in October 1743, no group was permitted to contain more than two sides from any one confederation other than the host [[AYFVL]]. The four-pot seeded draw procedure, the first such procedure used at an FLLA World Cup, was retained at the [[1748 FLLA World Cup|1748 edition]] and at every subsequent FLLA World Cup until the seeding reform of 1751.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1743/final-draw|title=Procedures for the 1744 FLLA World Cup final draw|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=2 October 1743}}</ref>

The draw was conducted by FLLA general secretary Halver Onstead and presented by [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] broadcaster Mira Cardevani, with retired internationals from each of the seven confederations drawing the team names. The ceremony was televised by the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] domestic broadcaster and was relayed by 21 broadcasters across more than 80 countries.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1743/draw-ceremony|title=Official record of the 1744 FLLA World Cup final draw|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=5 December 1743}}</ref>

===Officials===
{{Main|1744 FLLA World Cup officials}}

The FLLA Referees Committee appointed 22 refereeing trios, each consisting of one referee and two assistants from the same national association, and four support pairs drawn from a combined pool of 16 nations. The selections were announced in two tranches between October 1743 and February 1744, following an assessment programme at the [[1743 FLLA Continental Champions Cup]] and at senior friendlies organised across the seven host cities. The 22 selected referees were drawn from 16 nations and represented all seven [[FLLA]] confederations, although no [[AYFVL]] referee was eligible to take charge of any match involving an Ayuman side under the host-association exclusion rules then in force.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1744/officials-announced|title=Match officials confirmed for the 1744 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 February 1744}}</ref>

The opening match was refereed by Sanjar Petrok of [[Wundry]], a [[QUFVL]] official appointed to the fixture in his fourth tournament as an international referee. The final was officiated by Tahito Marennas of [[Wundry]] ([[QUFVL]]), the first Wundrian referee to take charge of an FLLA World Cup final. The two semi-finals were taken by Liwen Tahnari of [[Inania]] ([[MAFVL]]) for the first semi-final and Vekram Olansi of [[Acetoa]] ([[ACFVL]] support pair) for the second.

==Squads==
{{Main|1744 FLLA World Cup squads}}

Each participating squad consisted of 22 players, two of whom were required to be goalkeepers, under the squad allocation in force since the [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 edition]]. Each participating national association was required to confirm its final 22-player squad with the FLLA no later than seven days before the opening match; late replacements were permitted in the event of serious injury at any time up to 24 hours before a team's first fixture. A total of 704 players were registered for the tournament, of whom 64 were goalkeepers.

The oldest player at the tournament was [[Easuhura|Easuhuran]] central defender Olen Tareki, who was 37 years and 312 days old at the start of the competition; the youngest was [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] forward Bertan Soreno (20 years and 51 days), who would go on to win the [[#Awards|Best Young Player]] award. The mean age of registered players across the tournament was 27.1 years.

The squad nominally registered as the oldest by mean age was the [[New Misos|New Misosan]] selection (28.9 years), with six outfield players above the age of 31 at registration; the youngest squad by mean age was the [[Ztesh|Zteshi]] selection (24.4 years), nine of whose 22 players were earning their first senior tournament call-ups. The [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] central midfielder and captain Cario Velarzo, appearing at his fourth FLLA World Cup after representing his country at the [[1732 FLLA World Cup|1732]], [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736]] and [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740]] editions, set the all-tournament record for repeat appearances by a single player at the FLLA World Cup, a record that would stand until equalled at the [[1752 FLLA World Cup|1752 edition]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/records/repeat-appearances|title=FLLA World Cup records: repeat appearances by individual players|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=10 August 1744}}</ref> The leading individual appearance maker of the tournament was [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] right-back Marec Toranzu, who played all seven of his country's matches in their entirety for a total of 660 minutes on the pitch (including the full 30-minute period of extra time in the [[#Final|final]]).

A total of fifteen players withdrew between the publication of preliminary squads in May 1744 and the FLLA's deadline of 30 May 1744, eleven on grounds of injury and four for personal or domestic reasons. The most senior late withdrawal was [[New Misos|New Misosan]] central defender Halmir Renkalain, who suffered a hamstring strain in a pre-tournament friendly on 23 May and was replaced by the 24-year-old Tovric Lemarz. Two players who had appeared in the [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 final]] in [[Seytinemas]], [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] goalkeeper Renar Carestano and [[New Misos|New Misosan]] forward Veram Sokri, retired from international football before the [[1748 FLLA World Cup|1748 edition]] following the conclusion of the 1744 tournament.

==Venues==
{{Main|1744 FLLA World Cup venues}}

Seven stadiums in seven host cities were used in the final tournament, all located in [[Lycroa]]. Three of the seven venues had been built specifically for the tournament or substantially redeveloped during the bidding period; the remaining four were existing top-flight venues that received targeted upgrades to seating and broadcasting facilities under FLLA Council resolution 1742/11. The seven-venue programme remained the largest single-host stadium plan in the competition's history until the ten-venue programme of the [[1752 FLLA World Cup|1752 edition]].

The geographic distribution of the seven venues was a central element of the [[#Host selection|Lycroan host bid]] and an explicit policy choice of the post-reunification federal government. Four venues — the Estadio Huifarn ([[Huifarn]]), the Estadio Dacorca ([[Dacorca]]), the Estadio Tianco ([[Tianco]]) and the Estadio Sorvaya ([[Sorvaya]]) — lay within the historic southern federal heartland of the Federal Republic. The remaining three venues — the Estadio Tatuiro ([[Tatuiro]]), the Estadio Fujanza ([[Fujanza]]) and the Estadio Liambra ([[Liambra]]) — were sited in constituent states of the former [[State of Lycroa]] integrated into the federal republic under the [[Lycroan reunification]] of September 1738, and were the first matches to be played at FLLA World Cup venues on the territory of the former northern state. The Estadio Tatuiro, in particular, had been substantially redeveloped in 1742–1743 specifically for the tournament under a federal grant from the post-reunification investment programme.

The opening match was held at the Estadio Dacorca in [[Dacorca]], the second-largest stadium in the host country, which also staged the second of two quarter-finals on 29 June. The final was held at the Estadio Huifarn in [[Huifarn]], a purpose-built venue of 75,000 seats inaugurated in March 1744 and the principal venue of the tournament. The two semi-finals were divided between the Estadio Tianco in [[Tianco]] and the Estadio Sorvaya in [[Sorvaya]]. The third-place playoff was held at the Estadio Tatuiro in [[Tatuiro]].

===Venue profiles===

The '''Estadio Huifarn''', in [[Huifarn]], was the largest venue at the tournament and the principal final venue. The stadium, designed by the architectural studio Vohra Tasvil and inaugurated by the head of state of [[Lycroa]] on 12 March 1744, was constructed on the site of the older Huifarn Civic Ground (closed 1742) on the western bank of the [[Huifarn]] river.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.larf.ly/venues/estadio-huifarn|title=Estadio Huifarn: history, design and inauguration|publisher=Lycroan Arraby Federation|date=12 March 1744}}</ref> The 75,000-seat ground hosted the [[#Final|final]], one of the two [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-finals]] played on 28 June, two [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] ties (between [[Lycroa]] and [[Siana]], and between [[Verusa]] and [[Merela Sta]]), and seven group-stage fixtures. The ground was the home stadium of the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] domestic-league club Huifarn Olympic from August 1744, having been transferred from federal to municipal ownership under the bid agreement of 1743.

The '''Estadio Dacorca''' in [[Dacorca]] was the second-largest venue at the tournament with a redeveloped capacity of 70,000 and the principal northern-host venue. The ground, originally opened in 1696 and extensively redeveloped between 1742 and 1744 to bring it within FLLA capacity guidance for opening fixtures, hosted the opening match between [[Lycroa]] and [[Trian]] on 6 June, one of the two [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-finals]] played on 28 June, one [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie, and three further group-stage fixtures.

The '''Estadio Tianco''' in [[Tianco]], a 64,000-seat stadium opened in 1738 and the regular home venue of the [[Lycroa]] national side, hosted the first of the two [[#Semi-finals|semi-finals]] between [[Lycroa]] and [[Sanagara]] on 2 July, one [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie, and eight group-stage fixtures. The '''Estadio Sorvaya''' in [[Sorvaya]], a 58,000-seat venue opened in February 1744 specifically for the tournament, hosted the second [[#Semi-finals|semi-final]] between [[New Misos]] and [[Easuhura]], one [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie, and seven group-stage fixtures.

The '''Estadio Tatuiro''' in [[Tatuiro]], a 52,000-seat venue completed in 1731 in commemoration of the centenary of the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] federation's regional reorganisation, hosted the [[#Third place playoff|third-place playoff]] between [[Sanagara]] and [[New Misos]] on 3 July, alongside one [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie and six group-stage fixtures. The remaining two venues, the Estadio Fujanza and the Estadio Liambra, each staged one [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie, one [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-final]] on 29 June, and eight group-stage fixtures.

===Team base camps===

Each of the 32 participating squads selected a base camp from a shortlist of 48 candidate sites circulated by the Lycroan Arraby Federation in October 1743. Most teams opted for camps in or around the larger host cities, with six squads basing themselves within a one-hour radius of [[Huifarn]], five near [[Dacorca]] and four each in or around [[Tianco]] and [[Sorvaya]]. The remaining thirteen were divided between the smaller host cities and the inland highland corridor between [[Fujanza]] and [[Liambra]], which became known during the tournament as the "Lemarra belt".

==Format==

The 32 qualified teams were divided into eight groups of four for the group stage, drawn at the [[#Final draw|final draw]] on 4 December 1743. Each group operated on a single round-robin basis, with each team playing three matches; teams were awarded three points for a win, one for a draw and none for a defeat. The top two teams from each group advanced to the [[#Knockout stage|knockout stage]] while the bottom two were eliminated. Tiebreakers between teams level on points were applied in the following order: overall goal difference, overall goals scored, head-to-head record, fair-play points, and, if necessary, a drawing of lots by the FLLA Organising Committee.

In the knockout stage, fixtures were single-elimination ties played over 90 minutes; ties level at the end of normal time were extended by a single 30-minute period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]] of two 15-minute halves, with a [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]] used to decide ties that remained level after extra time. Both semi-final losers contested a [[#Third place playoff|third-place playoff]] on 3 July 1744.

The 32-team field, eight-group format and seeded four-pot draw were retained substantially unchanged from the [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 edition]] under which the modern competition had been inaugurated. The two most substantive procedural changes for the 1744 edition were the introduction of the standardised four-pot seeded draw, replacing the partially regional seeding model used in 1740, and the formalisation of the host-association exemption from binding qualifying fixtures, both adopted under FLLA Council resolution 1743/4.

==Innovations==

The 1744 FLLA World Cup introduced a number of regulatory and presentational changes, several of which proved durable in the subsequent regulatory history of the competition. The tournament was the first FLLA World Cup held under the confederation-rotation policy adopted by the FLLA Council in February 1740, which reserved hosting rights for each four-year cycle to a single nominated confederation in turn; the policy was retained without amendment at the [[1748 FLLA World Cup|1748]], [[1752 FLLA World Cup|1752]] and [[1756 FLLA World Cup|1756]] editions, and was extended by the FLLA Council in 1757 to cover the period through the 1772 cycle. The competition was also the first to use the four-pot seeded draw model that became standard practice for FLLA World Cup tournaments until the seeding reform of 1751.

The 1744 tournament was the first FLLA World Cup at which a formal host-association exemption from binding qualifying fixtures was applied. Under the exemption, the host nation [[Lycroa]] was placed in [[AYFVL]] qualifying Group A but its matchday results were treated as friendlies for the purpose of advancement; the seven binding [[AYFVL]] qualification places were divided between the seven non-host group winners. The exemption was carried forward by the FLLA Council to subsequent editions without amendment and remains the standard provision for host-association participation in qualifying tournaments to the present day.

A third procedural change, the introduction of the standing FLLA Tactical Review Committee, was constituted under FLLA Council resolution 1743/9 in September 1743 and reported for the first time on the 1744 tournament in November 1744. The Tactical Review Committee's first report attributed the unusually low goal-per-match average of the 1744 edition to the widespread adoption of compact rear-defensive systems among the leading sides, and recommended a series of procedural changes to the laws of the game that were subsequently adopted by the [[FLLA]] in 1746.

==Opening ceremony==

The opening ceremony of the 1744 FLLA World Cup was held at the Estadio Dacorca on 6 June 1744, sixty minutes before the kick-off of the opening match between the hosts [[Lycroa]] and [[Trian]]. Directed by [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] stage producer Tomian Verardi and choreographed by Lucira Carenzo, the ceremony lasted 24 minutes and featured 640 dancers, 120 musicians and a massed entrance representing each of the seven continental confederations of the [[FLLA]]. The performance opened with a sequence depicting the historical migration routes of the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] coastal peoples across the eastern Ayuman seaboard, before transitioning to a portrayal of the seven confederations arrayed as a single concentric ring around the centre circle. The narrative centrepiece of the ceremony was a four-minute sequence titled '''''La Unión''''', staged immediately before the closing musical item, in which performers wearing the historical civic colours of the southern federal heartland and of the constituent states of the former [[State of Lycroa]] entered the stadium from opposite ends and converged at the centre circle beneath a single federal banner; the sequence was framed by the production as the official commemorative re-enactment of the [[Lycroan reunification]] of September 1738 and was performed in the presence of the surviving members of the federal commission that had ratified the reunification settlement. The [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] vocalist Sirena Mateilo, joined by the Dacorca Choral Society, performed the tournament's official theme song "Olas del Norte" as the closing item of the ceremony.

Attending dignitaries included the head of state of [[Lycroa]], the President of the FLLA Council, the heads of state of [[Easuhura]] and [[Verusa]], and 52 ambassadors and senior diplomatic representatives. The ceremony was broadcast live on radio by 23 partner broadcasters across 41 countries; a transcontinental relay arranged in coordination with the broadcasting consortium that had carried the [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 final]] enabled the opening ceremony to be heard in real time on every continent of Andah, the first such global broadcast of an FLLA World Cup opening ceremony.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lnb.ly/1744/opening-ceremony|title=Opening ceremony of the 1744 FLLA World Cup: production notes and broadcast record|publisher=Lycroan National Broadcaster|date=6 June 1744}}</ref>

==Group stage==

The 32 qualified teams were drawn into eight groups of four. Each group operated on a single round-robin basis, with each team playing three matches; the top two finishers in each group advanced to the [[#Knockout stage|knockout stage]] while the bottom two were eliminated. Group rankings were settled first on points (three for a win, one for a draw), then on goal difference and goals scored.

The group stage produced one perfect record: [[Sanagara]] in Group E and [[Finae]] in Group F took maximum points from their three matches, with [[Finae]] additionally finishing with the largest positive group-stage goal difference of the round at plus five. The biggest single-match upset of the round, and of the tournament as a whole, was the 4–1 victory for [[Areoix Lie]] over the [[NAFVL]] qualifying winners [[United Delet]] at the Estadio Huifarn on 14 June; recorded across a pre-tournament FLLA-ranking gap of 215 points, the result was described in the FLLA Tactical Review Committee's 1744 report as the most significant upset by ranking margin in the modern history of the competition. The hosts [[Lycroa]] advanced as runners-up in a tightly contested Group A behind [[Ohtina]], who took the only perfect group-stage record in the host nation's group on the basis of a 3–2 victory over [[Lycroa]] at the Estadio Tatuiro on 10 June.

All times listed are Lycroan Coastal Time ([[wikipedia:UTC+02:00|LCT]], [[wikipedia:UTC|UTC]]+2).

==Knockout stage==

The knockout stage involved the sixteen teams that advanced from the group stage. Matches still level after 90 minutes were extended by a 30-minute period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]]; if scores remained tied after extra time, the tie was decided by [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]]. One of the eight round-of-sixteen ties required additional time and a second was decided on penalties, one of the four quarter-finals required additional time and was itself decided on penalties, and the [[#Final|final]] itself was decided on penalties after a goalless 120 minutes. The cumulative goal total of 22 across the sixteen knockout matches was widely cited at the time as evidence of the tactical caution that came to define the tournament.

===Round of 16===

The eight group winners were drawn against the eight group runners-up, with each match-up pairing teams from different groups. One of the eight ties required additional time, one was decided on penalties, and three further ties were settled by margins of a single goal. The highest-scoring fixture of the round was [[Easuhura]] 3–0 [[Finae]] at the Estadio Liambra, in which [[Easuhura|Easuhuran]] captain Tovi Renkalmar scored two of his side's goals; the lowest-scoring decisive fixture was the eventual champions' 1–0 victory over [[Siana]] at the Estadio Huifarn, settled in the 71st minute by [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] forward Galari Mestrei from a low cross by Bertan Soreno.

===Quarter-finals===

The four quarter-finals produced two ties decided in normal time, one in extra time and one on penalties. [[Lycroa]] beat [[Etirha]] 3–2 at the Estadio Huifarn, advancing through a 78th-minute winner by [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] forward Galari Mestrei that gave the hosts the lead for the third time in the match. [[Sanagara]] beat [[Quidic]] 4–3 on penalties after a 1–1 draw at the Estadio Dacorca, with [[Sanagara|Sanagaran]] goalkeeper Reol Khasimar saving the fifth Quidican kick to settle the longest shoot-out of the tournament. [[New Misos]] beat [[Ohtina]] 1–0 at the Estadio Fujanza through a single goal by Erron Petlik in the 49th minute. [[Easuhura]] beat [[Verusa]] 1–0 at the Estadio Liambra, with the only goal of the match scored by Tovi Renkalmar from a low cross by [[Easuhura|Easuhuran]] right-back Halmir Yaxri in the 24th minute.

===Semi-finals===

The first semi-final at the Estadio Tianco produced the highest-scoring knockout fixture of the tournament: the hosts [[Lycroa]] and [[Sanagara]] traded goals across both halves of normal time before [[Lycroa]] settled a 4–3 result through a 79th-minute strike from forward Galari Mestrei, his sixth and final goal of the competition. The match ended [[Sanagara]]'s otherwise unbeaten tournament run and gave [[Lycroa]] their first FLLA World Cup final appearance since the [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 edition]], in which they had been beaten 2–1 by [[New Misos]]. The second semi-final at the Estadio Sorvaya was decided inside 90 minutes by a single goal: [[Easuhura]] beat the defending champions [[New Misos]] 1–0 through a 58th-minute strike from captain Tovi Renkalmar, who turned in a low cross from right-winger Halmir Yaxri at the near post. The result eliminated the defending champions one round before the final and gave [[Easuhura]] their first FLLA World Cup final appearance in the competition's history.

===Third place playoff===

The third-place playoff was contested between the two losing semi-finalists at the Estadio Tatuiro on 3 July. [[Sanagara]] beat the defending champions [[New Misos]] 2–1 to take third place at the tournament, with goals from Maharan Soldai and Olen Marhan either side of a [[New Misos|New Misosan]] equaliser by Erron Petlik. The result gave [[Sanagara]] their highest finish at an FLLA World Cup in the competition's history and made [[New Misos]] the first defending champions in FLLA World Cup history to finish fourth at the subsequent tournament, an outcome [[New Misos]] would repeat at the [[1752 FLLA World Cup|1752 edition]] in defence of their [[1748 FLLA World Cup|1748 title]].

===Final===
{{Main|1744 FLLA World Cup final}}

The final was contested between the hosts [[Lycroa]] and [[Easuhura]], the Group A runners-up and Group E runners-up respectively, on 4 July 1744 at the Estadio Huifarn in [[Huifarn]] in front of an attendance of 74,500. [[Lycroa]] entered the match having scored thirteen goals across their six previous fixtures, while [[Easuhura]] had reached the final without conceding more than two goals in any single match. The match opened cautiously, with both sides defending in compact mid-block shapes and producing only three combined shots on target across the opening 45 minutes. [[Lycroa]] enjoyed a marginal territorial advantage in the second half but were unable to convert two clear chances, the first by forward Galari Mestrei from a tight angle in the 58th minute and the second by Bertan Soreno from a free kick on the edge of the penalty area in the 73rd minute; [[Easuhura]]'s clearest chance, an attempted volley by captain Tovi Renkalmar from a corner in the 81st minute, was deflected off target by [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] central defender Marec Toranzu.

The match remained goalless through normal time and through the two halves of extra time, with both sides defending in increasingly compact shapes and producing only a single shot on target between them across the 30-minute additional period. The tie was decided by a penalty shoot-out, the first FLLA World Cup final in the competition's history to be settled in this way and the only FLLA World Cup final ever to be decided on penalties without a single goal having been scored on either side during normal time or extra time. [[Lycroa]] won the shoot-out 3–0 after [[Easuhura|Easuhuran]] forward Tovi Renkalmar saw his first kick saved by [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] goalkeeper Hiren Quartelar, central defender Olen Tareki struck the crossbar with the second kick of the sequence, and right-back Halmir Yaxri saw his third kick saved low to Quartelar's right. The win gave [[Lycroa]] their fifth FLLA World Cup title, extending their record as the most successful nation in the competition's history.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1744/final-report|title=Match report: 1744 FLLA World Cup final, Lycroa 0–0 Easuhura (3–0 pens)|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=5 July 1744}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lnb.ly/sport/1744/final|title=Lycroa win fifth world title in goalless final at Huifarn|publisher=Lycroan National Broadcaster|date=4 July 1744}}</ref>

==Statistics==

===Goalscoring===

[[Lycroa]] finished as the tournament's leading goalscoring nation with 13 goals across seven matches, ahead of third-placed [[Sanagara]] (12 in seven) and fourth-placed [[New Misos]] (11 in seven). The overall goal-per-match average of 2.64 was the second-lowest then recorded at any FLLA World Cup, lower only than the 2.30 per match average of the [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 edition]], and prompted the FLLA Tactical Review Committee, in a report published in November 1744, to attribute the figure to the widespread adoption of compact rear-defensive systems among the leading sides and to the increasing standardisation of the offside trap as a defensive tactic in international play. The Tactical Review Committee's findings led directly to the procedural amendments to the laws of the game adopted by the [[FLLA]] in 1746.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1746/laws-of-the-game-amendments|title=Procedural amendments to the laws of the game arising from the 1744 Tactical Review|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 February 1746}}</ref>

===Discipline===

The FLLA Disciplinary Committee issued a total of 174 yellow cards and 9 red cards across the 64 matches of the tournament, an average of 2.72 yellows and 0.14 reds per match. The most-cautioned team was [[Etirha]], with 13 yellow cards and 1 red across their five matches; [[Trian]] received the fewest among the participating teams, with two yellows and no reds across their three matches, helping the team win the [[#Awards|FLLA Fair Play Trophy]]. Three players received red cards in the knockout stage: one in the round of sixteen and two in the quarter-finals.

==Awards==

The Best Player award, formally titled the FLLA Vairan Ball, was awarded by a panel of seven sports journalists drawn from each of the seven confederations to [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] central midfielder and captain Cario Velarzo, who anchored the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] midfield across all seven matches of the champions' run to the title and converted the opening kick of the final shoot-out. Velarzo was the first [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] player to receive the award, and his selection coincided with the formal recognition of his all-tournament record for repeat appearances by a single player at an FLLA World Cup.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1744/golden-ball-panel|title=FLLA Vairan Ball panel announces 1744 award|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=8 July 1744}}</ref>

Galari Mestrei of [[Lycroa]] took the FLLA Marskval with six personal strikes across the tournament, equalling the six-goal tally of [[New Misos|New Misosan]] forward Veram Sokri at the [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 edition]] and reflective of the unusually low overall scoring at the 1744 edition. The Bastion, awarded to the tournament's best goalkeeper, went to [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] goalkeeper Hiren Quartelar, who conceded just five goals across his country's seven matches, kept clean sheets in the round of sixteen and across normal and extra time in the final, and saved two of the three [[Easuhura|Easuhuran]] kicks taken in the final shoot-out (the third striking the crossbar). The Best Young Player Award was given to [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] forward Bertan Soreno, who at 20 years and 51 days at the start of the tournament was the youngest registered player at the competition; Soreno started six of [[Lycroa]]'s seven matches, scored three goals (including the 58th-minute strike that gave [[Lycroa]] a 3–2 lead against [[Sanagara]] in the [[#Semi-finals|semi-final]]), and converted the decisive third [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] kick of the [[#Final|final shoot-out]]. [[Trian]] received the Fair Play award after finishing the tournament with the fewest disciplinary points of any of the 32 participating teams.

==Preparations and costs==

The total budget allocated to the 1744 FLLA World Cup by the Lycroan Arraby Federation and the federal government of [[Lycroa]] was {{lahn}}760&nbsp;million. Of this, {{lahn}}460&nbsp;million was directed towards stadium construction and renovation across the seven venues, {{lahn}}180&nbsp;million towards transport upgrades (principally the [[Huifarn]]–[[Dacorca]] coastal rail corridor and arterial road improvements connecting the seven host cities), and {{lahn}}120&nbsp;million towards operational expenditure including security, broadcasting infrastructure and the volunteer programme. Per-venue capital costs averaged {{lahn}}66&nbsp;million across the seven stadiums, a figure later cited by FLLA reviewers as broadly in line with comparable single-host editions despite the unusually large stadium plan.

Three of the seven venues, comprising the Estadio Huifarn, the Estadio Sorvaya and the Estadio Tatuiro, were either newly built or extensively redeveloped for the tournament. The newest, Estadio Huifarn, was inaugurated on 12 March 1744, three months before the opening match. Total stadium construction overran the original budget by 8&nbsp;per&nbsp;cent, primarily because of cost escalation at the Estadio Huifarn and the Estadio Sorvaya; the federal government absorbed the overrun under a guarantee provision agreed with the Lycroan Arraby Federation at the bid stage in October 1742.

The combined security operation involved 18,000 police and military personnel deployed across the seven host cities, the largest such single-nation deployment in the competition's history at the time. No serious incidents were reported during the competition. A dedicated public transport extension programme, providing free local-network travel to ticket holders for the day of each match, was introduced for the duration of the tournament and was retained by several host municipalities as a permanent matchday provision following the closing ceremony.

Total tournament revenue, audited by the FLLA in August 1744, was {{lahn}}1.14&nbsp;billion, against costs of {{lahn}}760&nbsp;million, yielding a net surplus of {{lahn}}380&nbsp;million. The FLLA's standard 18&nbsp;per&nbsp;cent host-association allocation returned {{lahn}}205&nbsp;million to the Lycroan Arraby Federation, which was retained in full by the federation under the single-host allocation formula then in force.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/audit/1744-final-accounts|title=Audited final accounts of the 1744 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=26 August 1744}}</ref>

==Marketing==
{{Main|1744 FLLA World Cup marketing}}

The marketing programme for the 1744 FLLA World Cup was overseen by the Lycroan Arraby Federation in partnership with the FLLA's commercial division, with creative direction by the [[Huifarn]]-based studio Lopetu Diseño. The programme included the official emblem, mascot, match ball and theme song (see [[#Symbols|Symbols]] below), a domestic travelling-trophy tour that visited 21 cities across [[Lycroa]] in the year preceding the tournament, and a tiered sponsorship structure of four worldwide partners, eight host-nation partners and four regional supporters. Total sponsorship revenue across all three tiers was {{lahn}}340&nbsp;million, then the highest gross sponsorship figure recorded by any FLLA World Cup.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/commercial/1744-sponsorship|title=1744 FLLA World Cup commercial and sponsorship summary|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 September 1744}}</ref>

==Symbols==
{{Main|1744 FLLA World Cup symbols}}

===Emblem===

The official emblem of the tournament, designed by the [[Huifarn]]-based studio Lopetu Diseño, was unveiled on 4 June 1743 in a public ceremony at the Lycroan National Theatre in [[Huifarn]]. The design depicts the silhouette of a single trophy rising from a stylised coastal landscape, framed by seven radial bands representing the seven continental confederations of the [[FLLA]]. The radial-band motif was drawn from the heraldry of the historic [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] coastal provinces and was intended to symbolise the host nation's reception of the global tournament. The emblem received the FLLA Council's formal endorsement in October 1743 after a four-week consultation period with the seven confederations.

===Mascot===

The official mascot of the 1744 FLLA World Cup, named '''Maritello''', is an anthropomorphic eastern-coast seabird dressed in a red-and-white panel jersey representing the national colours of [[Lycroa]]. The mascot was selected by a domestic public vote organised by the Lycroan Arraby Federation in the spring of 1743, with three candidate designs presented to voters across the host nation and in print; Maritello prevailed over a stylised mountain ibex ("Lemarro") and a coastal hawk ("Tovielo") with 48&nbsp;per&nbsp;cent of the 1.9 million votes cast.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1743/mascot-vote|title=Maritello named official mascot of 1744 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[AYFVL]]|date=14 May 1743}}</ref>

===Match ball===

The official match ball, manufactured by the [[Dacorca]]-based sports equipment maker Mestrei Sport, was branded the '''Costera'''. The Costera featured a 32-panel hand-stitched construction in a red-and-white livery, a presentation chosen to evoke the coastal motif of the tournament emblem. The ball was the first FLLA World Cup match ball to use the now-standard 32-panel hand-stitched construction; the design pattern was retained at every FLLA World Cup through to the [[1752 FLLA World Cup|1752 edition]]. A distinct gold-coloured version of the ball, the Costera Final, was used in the final, the third-place playoff and the two semi-finals.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mestreisport.ly/products/costera-1744|title=Costera and Costera Final: official match balls of the 1744 FLLA World Cup|publisher=Mestrei Sport|date=15 February 1744}}</ref>

===Permanent trophy===

The permanent trophy of the 1744 FLLA World Cup, presented to the winners alongside the rotating [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]] at the closing ceremony of the final, was the '''Caltarra''', a 44-centimetre gilded silver sculpture commissioned by the Lycroan Arraby Federation from the [[Huifarn]]-based atelier Lopetu Diseño, the same studio responsible for the [[#Emblem|tournament emblem]]. The work depicts a stylised coastal wave breaking over a rendered representation of the seven continental confederations of the [[FLLA]] and takes its name from the historic Lycroan word ''caltarra'' (literally "kept thing"), in reference to the work's intended status as a permanent retention rather than a rotating award. The trophy was unveiled at the Lycroan National Theatre in [[Huifarn]] on 18 April 1744, six weeks before the opening match. Following the host nation's [[#Final|0–0 (3–0 pens) win]] over [[Easuhura]], the Caltarra was transferred to permanent retention by the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] federation and is displayed at the Huifarn National Museum.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1744/permanent-trophy|title=The Caltarra unveiled as 1744 FLLA World Cup permanent trophy|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 April 1744}}</ref>

===Theme song===

The official theme song of the tournament, "Olas del Norte" ("Waves of the North"), was composed by [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] musician Ruben Cardestar with lyrics jointly written by Cardestar and the vocalist Sirena Mateilo, who also performed the track. The studio recording was released on 12 March 1744 and topped the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] domestic charts across the months of April and May 1744, the first sports-themed track to lead the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] charts in the modern recording era.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.larf.ly/charts/1744-may|title=Lycroan domestic chart summary, May 1744|publisher=Lycroan Recording Industry Association|date=2 June 1744}}</ref>

==Media==
{{Main|1744 FLLA World Cup broadcasting rights}}

The 1744 FLLA World Cup was broadcast in 64 countries by 23 official radio partners and 6 official television partners, then the broadest cumulative international broadcasting reach of any FLLA World Cup. Domestic broadcasting rights in [[Lycroa]] were held by the Lycroan National Broadcaster (LNB), which produced the host radio feed and broadcast all 64 matches across its terrestrial radio network. The international rights for the [[AYFVL]] region were held by the [[Verusa|Verusan]] public-service broadcaster VRT; the [[ATFVL]] rights by the [[New Misos|New Misosan]] National Network (NMNN); and the [[QUFVL]] rights by a three-broadcaster consortium led by the Quidican National Network (QNN).

The 1744 edition was the first FLLA World Cup at which live television coverage was provided of the final; the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] domestic broadcaster carried the [[#Final|final]] on the Lycroan National Television (LNT) service to a domestic audience estimated at 4.1 million viewers, and onward television relays carried the match to limited audiences in [[Verusa]], [[Praesyu]] and [[New Misos]] in the days that followed. The transcontinental radio relay arrangement first used at the [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740 edition]] was extended in 1744 to cover all 64 matches; the FLLA reported a cumulative live broadcast audience for the tournament of 380 million individual listeners across all matches, with 140 million individuals tuning in to at least part of the final.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1744/audience-summary|title=1744 FLLA World Cup viewership summary|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 August 1744}}</ref>

===Attendance===

Cumulative attendance across the 64 matches of the tournament was 2,612,000 spectators, an average of 40,813 per match. The highest single-match attendance was the 74,500 recorded at the [[#Final|final]] between [[Lycroa]] and [[Easuhura]] at the Estadio Huifarn in [[Huifarn]], just below the stadium's listed all-seater capacity of 75,000; the lowest was the 33,200 attending the Group H fixture between [[Taval]] and [[Otiiric]] at the Estadio Tatuiro on 15 June.

Across the tournament, attendance averaged 48,300 in the knockout stage and 38,500 in the group stage. The three highest single-match attendances of the tournament were all recorded at the Estadio Huifarn, with the final, the QF1 between [[Lycroa]] and [[Etirha]], and the round-of-16 fixture between [[Verusa]] and [[Merela Sta]] all drawing crowds in excess of 72,000.

==Controversies==

The most prominent dispute of the tournament arose from the Group F fixture between the [[NAFVL]] qualifying winners [[United Delet]] and the [[ACFVL]] qualifier [[Areoix Lie]] at the Estadio Huifarn on 14 June, in which [[United Delet]] were defeated 4–1 in what was recorded across a pre-tournament FLLA-ranking gap of 215 points, the largest single-match ranking margin overturned at any FLLA World Cup of the modern era. The [[NAFVL]] secretariat lodged a formal complaint with the FLLA Disciplinary Committee on 16 June, contending that the appointment of an [[ACFVL]]-affiliated assistant referee to the match had created an inadvertent appearance of partiality; the FLLA Disciplinary Committee dismissed the complaint on 19 June, citing the absence of any specific impugned decision, and the result of the match was undisturbed.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/discipline/1744/nafvl-complaint|title=FLLA Disciplinary Committee ruling on NAFVL complaint of 16 June 1744|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=19 June 1744}}</ref> The [[United Delet]] head coach Halo Mastrar was dismissed by the United Delet Arraby Federation on 4 July 1744, the day of the final, after his side's elimination in the group stage on a points total of three from three matches.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nafvl.org/news/1744/mastrar-dismissal|title=Halo Mastrar dismissed as United Delet head coach|publisher=[[NAFVL]]|date=4 July 1744}}</ref>

A second incident, the dismissal of [[Etirha|Etirhan]] central defender Karne Vellaroth in the 73rd minute of the [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-final]] against the hosts [[Lycroa]] for a second bookable offence, was widely cited at the time as a notable refereeing call: the second yellow card was issued for what the [[Etirha|Etirhan]] Arraby Federation later contended in writing was an inadvertent collision rather than a deliberate trip. The FLLA Refereeing Committee declined to entertain the [[Etirha|Etirhan]] complaint on 30 June, citing the finality of on-field decisions under the laws of the game then in force; Vellaroth was suspended from any further matches at the tournament but as [[Etirha]] had been eliminated his absence was without sporting consequence.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/referees/1744/vellaroth-decision|title=FLLA Refereeing Committee decision on the Vellaroth dismissal|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=30 June 1744}}</ref>

A third dispute, of an administrative rather than sporting character, arose from the [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-final]] between [[Sanagara]] and [[Quidic]] at the Estadio Dacorca on 28 June, which went to penalty kicks after a 1–1 draw across normal and extra time. The shoot-out was extended to a fifth kick on each side, by which point [[Sanagara]] held a 4–3 advantage; the [[Quidic|Quidican]] Arraby Federation contended in a written submission to the FLLA on 1 July that the fifth [[Quidic|Quidican]] kick, taken by forward Karen Vekiri, had been disallowed in error by the referee on the grounds of an alleged step-back violation that the Federation contended was not a feature of the laws of the game then in force. The FLLA Refereeing Committee accepted the submission in principle on 8 July and issued a published clarification of the relevant provision of the laws on 14 July 1744, but declined to revisit the result of the match.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/referees/1744/vekiri-clarification|title=Clarification of laws on penalty-kick step-back violations|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 July 1744}}</ref>

==Aftermath==

[[Lycroa]]'s victory was their fifth FLLA World Cup title, extending their record as the most successful nation in the competition's history. The result was widely celebrated across [[Lycroa]], where the team's homecoming parade through central [[Huifarn]] on 7 July 1744 drew an estimated crowd of 2.1 million along a four-kilometre route from the Estadio Huifarn to the Lycroan federal palace.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lnb.ly/news/1744/homecoming-parade|title=Lycroan homecoming parade draws 2.1 million to Huifarn|publisher=Lycroan National Broadcaster|date=7 July 1744}}</ref> As reigning champions, [[Lycroa]] qualified automatically for the [[1748 FLLA World Cup|subsequent 1748 edition]] under the FLLA's defending-champion exemption then in force; [[Lycroa]] were drawn into the group stage at the 1748 tournament and were eliminated in the quarter-finals, ending the run of their immediate post-1744 generation.

Across the host nation, the tournament was judged a substantial organisational success and was widely framed in the Lycroan domestic press as the unambiguous consolidation moment of the [[Lycroan reunification]] of September 1738. The federal commission on national integration, in its final report of November 1744, identified the tournament's seven-city venue programme and the homecoming parade through [[Huifarn]] as the most visible and successful instruments of post-reunification federal cohesion to that date; the report's findings were cited by the federal government in support of the dissolution of the standing reunification commission with effect from 31 December 1744, six years after the September 1738 settlement.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gov.ly/1744/integration-commission-final-report|title=Final report of the federal commission on national integration|publisher=Federal Republic of Lycroa|date=18 November 1744}}</ref> An independent post-event report commissioned by the Lycroan federal government and published in November 1744 estimated the net economic contribution to the host economy at {{lahn}}1.6&nbsp;billion, against gross public expenditure of {{lahn}}760&nbsp;million across infrastructure and operations. International visitor arrivals across [[Lycroa]] over the tournament period totalled 510,000, the highest cumulative tournament-period visitor figure recorded in [[Ayuma]] up to that date. Of those arrivals, the [[AYFVL]] secretariat's separately reported figure of 47,000 visitors to the three former-State-of-Lycroa host cities ([[Tatuiro]], [[Fujanza]] and [[Liambra]]) was cited by the federal government as the largest single inflow of cross-border visitors to those municipalities since the September 1738 settlement. The matchday public transport provision introduced for the tournament was retained on a permanent basis after the closing ceremony by the municipal authorities of [[Huifarn]], [[Dacorca]] and [[Tianco]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ayfvl.org/1744/post-event-economic-impact|title=1744 FLLA World Cup post-event economic impact report|publisher=[[AYFVL]]|date=18 November 1744}}</ref>

The unusually low overall scoring at the tournament, with a goal-per-match average of 2.64 across the 64 fixtures, prompted the FLLA Tactical Review Committee's first published report in November 1744. The Committee's findings were instrumental in the procedural amendments to the laws of the game adopted by the [[FLLA]] in 1746, which included revisions to the offside rule and a tightening of the regulations governing time-wasting by goalkeepers. The Committee's report also recommended a review of the squad allocation system and the standing of the awards programme, both of which were partially implemented at the [[1748 FLLA World Cup|1748 edition]] and fully formalised at the [[1752 FLLA World Cup|1752 edition]] under FLLA Council resolution 1751/7.

The next edition of the FLLA World Cup, the [[1748 FLLA World Cup]], was awarded to a single-nation [[ATFVL]] bid from [[New Misos]] at the FLLA Council meeting of 4 March 1743, returning the tournament to [[Atirha]] for the first time under the confederation-rotation framework. [[New Misos]] would win the 1748 tournament on home soil, defeating [[Seytinemas]] 4–3 in a final later described in subsequent FLLA literature as the "Greatest World Cup in History".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/news/1743/1748-host-confirmation|title=New Misos confirmed as 1748 FLLA World Cup hosts under confederation-rotation framework|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=4 March 1743}}</ref>
